analysis.one_liner: Guarantees every Social Security beneficiary full benefits with annual cost-of-living increases through enforceable Treasury certificates.
analysis.headline: Two months after introduction, the bill has four Republican cosponsors and has seen no action in the House Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Treasury Department to send every Social Security beneficiary a certificate legally guaranteeing their full monthly benefit and at least an annual cost-of-living increase. Each certificate would count as a binding federal obligation not subject to yearly budget fights, and the bill would add mandatory funding to cover benefits once payroll taxes and trust fund reserves run short, which government trustees project around 2035. It was introduced in November 2025 and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action on it.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the roughly 70 million Americans who receive or will receive Social Security retirement, survivor, and disability benefits would get a legally enforceable Treasury certificate guaranteeing their full monthly benefit and at least an annual cost-of-living increase [S2] [S3]. Because the certificates count as binding budget authority, future Congresses could not legally scale back an individual's benefits to close the program's funding gap [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Within 90 days of enactment, Treasury would issue a legally enforceable certificate to every current beneficiary, and to each new beneficiary going forward, guaranteeing their full monthly benefit amount.
The certificate would guarantee benefits are increased at least annually based on an accurate cost-of-living determination, protecting recipients from inflation eroding their checks.

The certificates would constitute budget authority in advance of appropriations, meaning the government's obligation to pay full benefits would not depend on Congress passing spending bills each year.
The bill addresses the projected 2035 shortfall, when trustees say tax revenue and trust fund reserves will not cover full benefit payments, by providing additional mandatory funding.

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, the federal government would pay. Under the bill, each guarantee certificate counts as budget authority that does not depend on yearly appropriations, and the bill provides additional mandatory funding to cover benefits once payroll tax and trust fund reserves fall short, which CRS notes is projected around 2035 [S2]. That cost ultimately falls on federal taxpayers and the general treasury, since payroll taxes alone are projected not to cover full benefits [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill guarantees benefits without clearly solving how to pay for them: payroll taxes and reserves are projected to fall short in 2035, and the added mandatory funding would have to come from general federal revenue, higher borrowing, or taxes not specified in the bill.

Making full benefits binding budget authority would take away Congress's ability to adjust the program's financing, which could force larger deficits or abrupt tax increases later if the underlying shortfall is never addressed.

The promise of an 'accurate' cost-of-living adjustment tied to 'the individual' is vague in the bill text, leaving open how the increase would be calculated and whether it would be more generous than the current formula.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goal is popular and the core idea — making full Social Security benefits a legally enforceable guarantee rather than something a future Congress could trim — would matter a great deal to retirees if the funding gap arrives on schedule around 2035 [S2]. But the bill is a one-page guarantee that does not identify a serious revenue source for the added mandatory funding it invokes [S2] [S3], so as drafted it functions more as a statement of principle than a solvency plan. An honest supporter would acknowledge that a real fix requires saying who pays, and this bill does not.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in November 2025 and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Burchett introduced the bill on November 18, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which handles Social Security legislation.
Four other Republican members signed on as cosponsors; no Democrats have cosponsored the bill.
As of the latest recorded action, the committee has not held a hearing, marked up the bill, or sent it to the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has materially benefited yet: beneficiaries' benefits are unchanged and the solvency question is untouched. The only gain so far goes to the bill's sponsor and cosponsors, who can point to a stated position on protecting Social Security.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sponsor gains a position; no one else yet

for.name: Rep. Tim Burchett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and is its only sponsor.

for.name: Four Republican House members
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, the bill's only recorded support to date.

sides.party_line_note: The bill is sponsored only by Republicans (one sponsor and four Republican cosponsors) with no Democratic cosponsors and no votes yet, so no partisan split on the floor has been tested.

industries.note: No concentrated industry stands to gain or lose; the bill's cost would fall on the federal budget and taxpayers generally, while its benefit flows to retirees, disabled workers, and survivors.

analysis.trajectory: This is very likely to go nowhere. The bill has a single sponsor and four cosponsors, all Republicans, no Democratic support so far, and no committee action since referral in November 2025. The overwhelming majority of bills referred to committee never receive a markup or a floor vote, and a Social Security guarantee of this kind would need a funding plan that can pass both chambers, which this bill does not clearly provide. Its realistic role is as a statement of position heading into the 2035 trust fund shortfall debate.
